name: Apache Pekko
summary: The Apache-licensed fork of Akka 2.6: actors, cluster sharding, persistence, streams and HTTP for Java and Scala, run by a foundation instead of a company.
intro: Pekko works the way Akka 2.6 did. Each JVM runs an `ActorSystem` that drives many lightweight actors, each with a mailbox, handling one message at a time under a parent that supervises it. Pekko Cluster joins JVMs into a membership group, Cluster Sharding places each entity actor by ID on exactly one node and moves it when nodes come and go, and Pekko Persistence keeps each entity’s events in a journal (Cassandra, JDBC, R2DBC for PostgreSQL, DynamoDB) to replay after a restart. Separate modules add Streams, HTTP, gRPC, Projections, Management (cluster bootstrap and health checks on Kubernetes) and Connectors, the renamed Alpakka, including Kafka. Messages between actors are delivered at most once.

The code started from Akka 2.6.20, the last line before Lightbend moved Akka to the Business Source License. It differs from Akka mostly in names: packages are `org.apache.pekko`, config keys start with `pekko.`, node addresses use `pekko://` and the default remoting ports changed. Data persisted by Akka can be read by Pekko and the other way round, and mixed Akka and Pekko clusters are experimental. Jars are on Maven Central with no licence key or fee. The 1.x line (1.7.1, September 2026) runs on Java 8 and later; 2.0, in milestones not meant for production, needs Java 17, drops Scala 2.12 and brings in Akka code as each Akka release turns Apache 2.0.
strengths: Apache 2.0 under the Apache Software Foundation: no licence keys, no fees, and no single company that can change the licence
A short path from Akka 2.6: mostly renamed packages, config keys and ports, and persisted data stays readable
The full Akka 2.6 toolkit, with more than 50 libraries released: Core, HTTP, gRPC, Connectors, Kafka, Management, Persistence plugins and Projections
Used by Apache Flink (since 1.18) and the Play Framework
limits: Akka features added since 2022, such as Replicated Event Sourcing over gRPC, Akka Edge and Distributed Cluster, aren’t in released 1.x versions; the 2.0 line ports Akka code only once it turns Apache, three years after each Akka release
No vendor behind it: at incubation no company committed dedicated developers (Aiven and Altoo pledged to help as needed), so help comes from the community
Pekko 2.0 removes much deprecated code, so libraries built against 1.x are unlikely to work with it, and its milestones are for testing only
Apps already on Akka 2.7 or later may use APIs that Pekko 1.x doesn’t have, because the fork starts from 2.6
The usual actor-model costs: at-most-once delivery, versioned message serialization, cluster and split-brain operations, and JVM only

snippet.title: Move an Akka 2.6 project to Pekko 1.x: dependencies, packages, config and ports
source: # GNU sed and grep. 1. build.sbt: swap the organisation and artifact names
#    then set the versions by hand; Alpakka Kafka becomes "org.apache.pekko" %% "pekko-connectors-kafka"
# 2. packages: akka.* becomes org.apache.pekko.*, AkkaException becomes PekkoException
# 3. config: akka { ... } and akka.actor.provider become pekko { ... } and pekko.actor.provider
# 4. anything left: addresses (akka:// is now pekko://) and ports (Artery 25520 is now 17355)

sections.title: Akka or Pekko?
sections.intro: Both grew from the same code until Akka 2.6. The choice is mostly about licence and cost against the features Akka has added since.

rows.label: Licence
values: BSL 1.1 since 2.7 (October 2022); each release becomes Apache 2.0 three years after it ships

rows.label: Production use
values: Licence key required; free for organisations under $25 million revenue, OSS and academia, otherwise a subscription with no public price list

rows.label: Where the jars come from
values: Akka’s own repository through a tokenized URL (since Akka 23.10)

rows.label: Current stable line
values: Akka core 2.10.23 (September 2026), part of the Akka 25.10 bundle

rows.label: Java versions
values: 1.x: Java 8 and later; 2.0: Java 17 and later

rows.label: Added after the fork
values: Distributed Cluster, Projections and Replicated Event Sourcing over gRPC (23.05), Akka Edge (23.10), licence keys (2024)
Its own fixes and new stream operators; 2.0 milestones port Akka changes up to 2.8.4 so far

rows.label: Higher-level tools
values: Akka SDK and managed Serverless or BYOC hosting

rows.label: Who’s behind it
values: Lightbend, doing business as Akka, with commercial support
Apache committers; at incubation no company committed dedicated developers

rows.label: Coming from Akka 2.6
values: Upgrade in place; 2.7 and later need a licence key in production
Mostly renames; persisted data readable both ways; mixed clusters experimental

notes: Each Akka patch release has its own change date: 2.8.4 became Apache 2.0 on 15 August 2026, but 2.8.10 converts only in August 2029.

story: In September 2022 Lightbend announced that Akka 2.7 and later would ship under the Business Source License instead of Apache 2.0, and that Akka 2.6 would get security fixes only until September 2023. Projects built on Akka, including Apache Flink, needed an open-source way forward.

A group of Akka users and contributors, among them Matthew de Detrich, PJ Fanning, He Pin and Josep Prat, with Aiven and Altoo offering support, proposed forking the last Apache-licensed code into the Apache Incubator. They argued it was not a hostile fork but a continuation of the existing licence, and that an ASF home would protect it from another licence change. After a community vote they named it Pekko, after the Finnish god of farming. It entered incubation on 24 October 2022, released Pekko 1.0 in July 2023, and Flink 1.18 switched to it that October.

Pekko became a top-level Apache project in March 2024, by which time more than 50 libraries had been released. Its 2.0 line, in milestones since 2025, raises the minimum to Java 17 and pulls in Akka code as each release passes its change date.

choices.choice: Fork the last Apache-licensed release instead of rewriting
choices.why: Many applications ran on Akka 2.6. Starting from the same code meant moving to Pekko could be mostly a matter of renaming, and data persisted by Akka stayed usable.

choices.choice: Rename everything, down to ports and addresses
choices.why: The Akka name had to be removed from the code for trademark reasons. Pekko also changed the default remoting ports so they don’t clash with Akka’s, and uses `pekko://` addresses.

choices.choice: A home at the Apache Software Foundation
choices.why: The proposal argued that only foundation ownership would stop a repeat of the licence change, and that it would reassure Apache projects such as Flink that depended on Akka.

choices.choice: Take Akka code only after it turns Apache 2.0
choices.why: BSL code can’t go into an Apache project. Because each Akka release converts after three years, the 2.0 milestones add Akka changes as they are relicensed, up to Akka 2.8.4 so far.

timeline.text: Akka moves to the BSL; Pekko enters the Apache Incubator on 24 October
